notes.subject: car
notes.text: All car coverage is low-cam: a much bigger car blur and a lower view that makes roads look wide.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Fully white plates with no blue strip; front plates are very short, rear ones long or tall, with a red emblem left and canton emblem right.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Black and white bollards with white or grey reflectors, either wedge-shaped or cylindrical with a rounded top.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Main-road direction signs are blue and side roads are white; big towns are usually on blue.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian signs have seven stripes and are tall blue rectangles rather than squares.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Long yellow dashed road lines are a good clue.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Pedestrian crossings are painted yellow, which in Europe happens only here and next door.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Road signs often have a round, grey metal border around them.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Town entry signs are white or blue in a metal frame; the back may show distances and a canton abbreviation.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are black with a white arrow, rarely white with a black arrow.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Bus stop signs wrapped by thick metal signposts are unique to this country.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The south is extremely mountainous with long thin valleys; the north has large farms on flat or rolling land.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Light, warm-coloured stone buildings with wooden details, tiled gable roofs and two-part wooden shutters that open sideways.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Four official languages, split by region, with some bilingual areas. Signs vary accordingly, and the northern language never uses ß.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Two-letter canton abbreviations appear on town entry signs and on the start of unblurred plates.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: The first digit of postal codes rises from west to east.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Exposed limestone rocks on forested hills and many rock walls mark the Jura mountains.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Smooth orange-yellow stone, tiled roofs and green or brown Mediterranean-style shutters point to the southern, Italy-border region.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Elaborate timber frames, often painted red, are common in the northeast.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Living house joined at 90 degrees to a long barn, with a facade of small squares each holding one window.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: All-stone houses with white decorative paint around windows and corners.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Olive green signposts, sign borders and sign backs are typical of Basel-Landschaft.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Thick wooden bollards, square or cylindrical, are common in Valais.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Reflectors are attached to roadside fences instead of bollards in Glarus.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: A simplified bike symbol of a person over two disconnected wheels appears around Geneva and the Martigny valley.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The wide flat valley of Martigny has the country's densest fruit plantations with big mountains either side.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Unique train coverage on the Bernina Express line runs through Graubünden down to Tirano in Italy.
